question.text: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[4]{1-x}}$ about $x=0$ is
question.explanation:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give \[ P_2(x) = f(0) + f'(0)(x-0) +\dfrac{1}{2}f''(0)(x-0)^2. \]

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ and $f''(0)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f(x) &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[4]{1-x}} = (1-x)^{-1/4} &\Longrightarrow&& f(0) &= 1\\[3pt] f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)^{-5/4} &\Longrightarrow&& f'(0) &= \frac{1}{4}\\[3pt] f''(x) &= \dfrac{5}{16}(1-x)^{-9/4} &\Longrightarrow&& f''(0) &= \frac{5}{16} \end{align*}

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ and $f''(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives \begin{align*} P_2(x)&=1+\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\cdot x+\left(\dfrac{5}{16}\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\\[5pt] &=1 + \frac{1}{4}x + \frac{5}{32}x^2. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial $P_2(x)$ of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt{2}\,x}$ about $x=0.$
question.explanation:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$ P_2(x) = f(0) + f'(0)(x-0) +\dfrac{1}{2}f''(0)(x-0)^2. $$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ and $f''(0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x) &= \dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt{2}\,x}=(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-1} &\Longrightarrow&& f(0) &= 1\\[3pt] f'(x) &= \sqrt{2}(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-2} &\Longrightarrow&& f'(0) &= \sqrt{2}\\[3pt] f''(x) &= 4(1-\sqrt{2}\,x)^{-3} &\Longrightarrow&& f''(0) &= 4 \end{align*}

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ $f'(0),$ and $f''(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

\begin{align*} P_2(x) &=1+\sqrt{2}\,x+4\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}+\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sqrt{2}}\,x+\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}\,x^2. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial $P_2(x)$ of $f(x)=\dfrac{4}{x}$ about $x=2.$
question.explanation:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=2,$ we plug $a=2$ into the general formula to give $$ P_2(x) = f\left(2\right) + f'\left(2\right)\left(x - 2\right) +\dfrac{1}{2}f''\left(2\right)\left(x-2\right)^2. $$

So, we need to work out $f\left(2\right),$ $f'\left(2\right),$ and $f''\left(2\right)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f(x) &= \dfrac{4}{x} &\Longrightarrow&& f\left(2\right) &= 2\\[5pt] f'(x) &= -\dfrac{4}{x^2} &\Longrightarrow&& f'\left(2\right) &= -1\\[5pt] f''(x) &= \dfrac{8}{x^3} &\Longrightarrow&& f''\left(2\right) &= 1 \end{align*}

We now plug the results for $f\left(2\right),$ $f'\left(2\right),$ and $f''\left(2\right)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives \begin{align*} P_2(x) &= 2+(-1)\left(x-2\right)+1\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x-2\right)^2\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2} - \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}\left(x-2\right) + \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{2}}\left(x-2\right)^2. \end{align*}

question.text: What is the coefficient of $x^2$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+4x}$ at $x = 0?$
question.explanation:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$ P_2(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2}x^2. $$

The coefficient of $x^2$ in the above Taylor polynomial is

$$ \dfrac{f''(0)}{2}. $$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative $f''(x)$:

\begin{align*} f(x)&=\dfrac{1}{1+4x}=(1+4x)^{-1}\\[5pt] f'(x)&=-4(1+4x)^{-2}\\[5pt] f''(x)&=32(1+4x)^{-3} \end{align*}

Then, we evaluate $f''(x)$ at $x=0.$ This gives

$$ f''(0)=\dfrac{32}{(1+4\cdot 0)^{3}}=32. $$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $x^2,$ as follows:

$$ \eqalign{ \dfrac{f''(0)}{2}&=\dfrac{32}{2}=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{16} } $$

question.text: What is the coefficient of $x^2$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\cos(2x)$ at $x = 0?$
question.explanation:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by $$ P_2(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2}x^2. $$

The coefficient of $x^2$ in the above Taylor polynomial is $$ \dfrac{f''(0)}{2}. $$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative $f''(x)$: \begin{align*} f(x)&=\cos(2x)\\[5pt] f'(x)&=-2\sin(2x)\\[5pt] f''(x)&=-4\cos(2x) \end{align*}

Then, we evaluate $f''(x)$ at $x=0.$ This gives

$$ f''(0)=-4\cos(2\cdot 0)=-4. $$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $x^2,$ as follows:

$$ \eqalign{ \dfrac{f''(0)}{2}&=\dfrac{(-4)}{2}=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-2} } $$
